theory.intro: A line of best fit is fitted to **all** the points, so a single **outlier** — a point well away from the main trend — can pull the line away from the pattern. Removing it can change the gradient, but need not do so.
facts: An **outlier** lies far from the main trend of the other points, on either side of where the line of best fit would otherwise sit.

The result depends on the outlier's position and the remaining data. Removing an outlier can make a line steeper or less steep, leave its gradient unchanged, or change its direction. For a negative gradient, **steeper** means more negative. Keep each illustrated line within the horizontal range of its data.
steps: Identify the outlier: the point that sits far from the trend of the other points
Compare the displayed line with the trend of the remaining points: consider whether the outlier makes the line steeper or flatter, for either a positive or a negative trend
State how removal changes the gradient: steeper, less steep or unchanged; check whether its direction also changes

workedExamples.solution_text:
The outlier is $(1,10)$: it lies far above the upward trend of the other points.

It pulls the low-$x$ end of the fitted line upward, flattening it. Removing it makes the gradient more positive and steeper.

The outlier is $(6,12)$: it lies far above the main upward trend.

It pulls the high-$x$ end upward, making the fitted line steeper than the remaining trend. Removing it makes the gradient less steep; it remains positive.

The outlier is $(6,11)$: it lies far above the downward trend of the other points.

It pulls the right-hand end upward, flattening the downward line. Removing it makes the gradient more negative and steeper.

The outlier is $(1,13)$.

It pulls the low-$x$ end upward, making the downward fitted line steeper than the trend of the remaining points. Removing it makes the gradient less negative and less steep.

The effect depends on the outlier's position relative to the main trend.
